newsitem.title: USA: IMM currency futures end mixed, yen, marks higher.
newsitem.headline: IMM currency futures end mixed, yen, marks higher.

text.p: IMM currencies ended mixed, as yen and marks clung to gains despite expectations for a U.S. interest rate hike next week, traders and analysts said.
"You have to buy yield and yield is in the U.S., that's the bottom line," Rob Fullem, a currency analyst at NatWest Markets, said.

While the foreign exchange markets have priced in a 25-basis-point U.S. rate hike on March 25, Fullem said the Federal Open Market Committee could decide at Tuesday's meeting to leave rates steady or raise rates 50 basis points.
"They could easily surprise everyone," he said.

Not only is the market uncertain about the direction of U.S. monetary policy, but the market still remains perplexed about the U.S. administration's commitment to a strong dollar policy, forex market sources said.
"The volatilities (on forex options) are going up, because you have a number of things coming up in the next several weeks," Fullem said.

The market's skittishness regarding the U.S.'s dollar policy was underscored on Friday morning when a news agency reported that Federal Reserve vice chairwoman Alice Rivlin said excessive strength in the dollar punishes exporters.
The Federal Reserve said that Rivlin did not say there were limits on U.S. Treasury secretary Robert Rubin's support for a strong dollar, and that Rubin was the spokesman on the dollar.

However, June yen and marks held a firm tone, possibly digesting Thursday's U.S. trade data which showed the U.S. trade deficit for February widened against both Japan and China. Overall U.S. exports fell 0.6 percent. "There is no doubt about it," Fullem said. "The number wasn't good for the dollar."
The report raised concerns that U.S. manufacturing sector could exert pressure on the U.S. administration to slow the dollar's ascent.
On Friday the U.S. automakers association repeated concerns that the strong dollar/yen was hurting efforts to boost auto and parts exports into Japan.
"I don't think the U.S. has a clear cut policy," Fullem said.
However, Fullem said Vice President Albert Gore could comment on the dollar during his eight-day Asian tour which begins on Saturday.

At the end of pit trade, June yen was up $0.000057 at $0.008237, marks were up $0.0022 at $0.5966, Swiss francs were off $0.0024 at $0.6924, sterling was $0.0110 higher at $1.6024, Canadian dollars were off $0.0002 at $0.7291, Australian dollars were $0.0012 lower at $0.7854 and Mexican pesos were up $0.000150 at $0.121600.
